title: Prompting Change with GenAI in Large-Scale Document Review: A Real-World Study
pub: Journal of Technology Law & Policy, vol. 30, issue 2
author: Robert Keeling · Ray Mangum · Amy Hanke · Alyssa Ogden

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s supervised, task-specific approach and materially extends it with real-world client-data evidence from bounded document-review tasks. It reports potential gains over manual review and search terms while emphasizing monitoring, tailored workflows, quality controls and broader validation rather than general legal autonomy.
qs: Even with those open questions, the proof-of- concept findings in this Article provide a meaningful starting point: they suggest that, when appropriately deployed and monitored, genAI can exceed what is possible with manual review and search terms.

The genAI revolution in legal practice is still in its early stages, and additional empirical research will be important to test, validate, and refine the results reported here across a wider range of matters, document types, workflows, and risk profiles.

st.t: TAR governance: Reduced review retains legal judgment
st.an: The source accepts e-discovery and TAR as evidence that technology can improve large-scale review through defensible, human-trained processes, then materially extends the proposition with a real-matter GenAI comparison. Its strong relevance results, mixed issue-coding performance, and call for broader testing reinforce the cluster’s emphasis on task-specific validation rather than universal superiority, although its prediction of inevitable GenAI adoption is more confident than the evidence establishes.
qs: The results varied depending on document type, but overall, the relevance review produced a high recall rate of 83.9% and a precision rate of 84.7%.
The profession needs more empirical data to test that claim— to evaluate whether genAI truly delivers on its potential across varying types of legal matters and document sets.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The study accepts the cluster’s core proposition and materially strengthens it with real-world evidence from large-scale document review. It demonstrates strong but bounded performance on first-level responsiveness review, alongside task, document-context and technical limitations that make prompt refinement, selective deployment, verification and human quality control necessary.

kp.k: Single-matter study tests AI against attorney document coding
kp.d: Keeling, Mangum, Hanke and Ogden tested Relativity’s aiR for Review using a corporate client’s closed regulatory-subpoena matter. The protocol selected 1,600 custodial documents stratified by custodian and document type and a separate 200-document workpaper sample. Approximately 6% of the population was excluded because extracted text was absent, under .05 KB or over 150 KB. The authors understood the tool to use GPT-4o May 2024. These are findings from one tool and matter, not a cross-market comparison.
qs: including a sample of 1,600 custodial documents, stratified by custodian and document type.
A similar, separate sample of 200 previously coded documents was identified for the population of workpapers.
During the time of the study, the authors understood that Relativity aiR products were using GPT-4o May 2024.

kp.k: Prompt refinement and human validation underpin reported performance
kp.d: Attorneys adapted the original human review protocol into prompts and refined them through two fifty-document rounds, addressing over-reliance on industry terminology. For final responsiveness metrics, two attorneys who led the original review re-coded the entire 1,600-document sample, splitting it without duplicate review, with instructions not to defer to AI or prior coding and with written explanations. Their decisions supplied the human gold standard.
qs: The study team then worked to iteratively refine the prompt by evaluating its performance on small samples of fifty documents, making revisions based on the results of each round.
The two conflict reviewers split the 1,600-document set between them without duplication in the review.
Each reviewer provided written notes explaining the basis for coding decisions on each document.

kp.k: Custodial responsiveness review achieved 83.9% recall, 84.7% precision
kp.d: Of 1,600 custodial documents, the gold standard identified 559 as responsive. AI predicted 554 responsive, comprising 469 true positives and 85 false positives; 600 were predicted not responsive, including 10 responsive documents. The authors report 83.9% recall and 84.7% precision when borderline documents are excluded from production; the recall denominator still includes all 559 responsive documents. They characterize performance as on par with attorneys for identifying responsive documents while producing fewer false positives, and compare it with commonly accepted TAR recall levels rather than reporting a same-sample TAR test.
qs: the calculated recall rate was 83.9% (469/559) and the precision rate was 84.7% (469/554).
identifying actually responsive documents on par with attorney reviewers while generating fewer false positives than attorney reviewers.
The baseline recall of 83.9% compares favorably to state-of-the-art performance metrics for traditional TAR models where a 70–75% recall rate is widely considered acceptable.

kp.k: Borderline inclusion trades precision for substantially higher recall
kp.d: AI classified 368 documents, or 23.0% of the custodial sample, as borderline; human validation found 69 responsive and 299 nonresponsive. Treating borderline predictions as responsive increased recall to 96.2% but reduced precision to 58.4%. The authors emphasize that this workflow decision increases responsive-document capture at the expense of false positives and potentially review cost.
qs: When borderline documents were included as responsive predictions, recall increased to 96.2% ((469+69)/559) but precision dropped to 58.4% ((469+69)/(554+368)).

Including the borderline documents can increase the number of responsive documents identified, while potentially materially increasing the number of false positives and thus increasing the cost of the review.

kp.k: Junk classifications and processing errors require attention
kp.d: Of 62 documents classified as junk, two were responsive; nine of the 16 documents ultimately returning errors were responsive. Initially 26 documents errored; a rerun eliminated ten unknown errors, while a third attempt did not resolve more. One error reported an ungrounded citation, which the authors describe as suggesting a potential hallucination, not a measured general hallucination rate.
qs: Additionally, genAI classified 62 documents as junk, of which 2 were determined responsive.
Of the 16 documents for which genAI returned an error, 9 were determined responsive by the gold standard review.

Details for one document listed “ungrounded citations detected in completion,” which indicates that the genAI tool generated a citation that cannot be found in the document’s text—suggesting a potential AI hallucination.

kp.k: Issue tagging yielded mixed, task-dependent results
kp.d: The same 1,600 custodial documents were tested against ten common issue tags. Conflict reviewers examined 380 documents with at least one AI–attorney disagreement: 167 conflicts were resolved fully for AI, 126 fully for the original reviewer and 87 had mixed resolutions. The authors report that text-driven determinations worked fairly well, whereas metadata-dependent or structured-content tasks performed much worse. Date-limited Issue #1 generated excessive positives because the tool could not distinguish years; spreadsheets and charts contributed to low recall for Issue #5.
qs: At a document level, conflicts for 167 documents (43.9%) were resolved fully in favor of genAI.
Conflicts were resolved fully in favor of the reviewer for 126 documents (33.2%).

Where the issue coding depended on metadata, structured content (e.g., spreadsheets or templates/forms), or documents without sufficient text (e.g., images), genAI’s issue analysis performed much worse.

kp.k: Workpaper limitations prevented completion of planned issue analysis
kp.d: After applying issue prompts to fifty workpapers, the team concluded that the tool was ineffective for this industry-specific document type and did not run the full 200-document sample. Human reviewers had contextual cover pages and linked supporting documents that single-document extracted-text analysis could not consider. Templates, poor text conversion and missing checkbox states created further interpretive problems.
qs: the study team determined that genAI was not an effective tool for issue coding this particular type of industry-specific document at the time of the study.
Accordingly, the analysis was not run on the full 200-document sample.
Checklists were especially problematic, as checked boxes are not represented in the extracted text, further complicating genAI’s ability to analyze the information accurately.

kp.k: AI can replace first-level tasks while retaining oversight
kp.d: The authors recommend conditional use for first-level responsiveness review of text-based documents, prioritization for attorney review and quality control after human review. They particularly identify detection of attorney false positives as a promising quality-control application that could reduce production of nonresponsive material. These are workflow recommendations, not findings that entire legal roles can be eliminated.
qs: The results can be used in a variety of ways, ranging from replacing first-level review, identifying documents to prioritize for human review, or conducting quality control of human reviewers.

Although genAI tools may serve as a defensible and efficient component of the eDiscovery workflow in appropriate cases, human oversight and quality-control checks remain important to ensure accuracy and reliability.

kp.k: Cost savings remain conditional rather than quantified
kp.d: The article proposes potentially significant savings versus manual review but does not report a monetary saving. It identifies eligibility rates, restrictions on substituting AI for sensitive or C-suite documents, sampled versus comprehensive human quality control, request complexity and prompt-refinement time as determinants. Reported tool runtime was approximately three minutes for fifty documents and 35 minutes for 1,600, rather than a complete end-to-end review-time comparison. ESI-protocol negotiations and disputes over transparency or validation could offset efficiency gains.
qs: Run time for sets of 50 documents was approximately 3 minutes, for both Relevance and Issue Analysis. Run time for the set of 1,600 was approximately 35 minutes.
Cost savings would also be higher where second- level quality control by human reviewers is limited to a sample rather than the entire document set.
could lead to contentious and costly negotiations, potentially making it more expensive than traditional approaches at this point in time.

kp.k: Tailored preprocessing can address some context limitations
kp.d: Recommended safeguards include excluding technically unsuitable files, examining extracted-text quality, filtering on metadata where dates or other external attributes determine relevance, and assessing economical ways to restore family context. For the workpapers, the authors propose merging cover-page and document text as a possible workaround; they do not report testing its effectiveness.
qs: the team could have created a version of extracted text that merged the cover page and document text for purposes of the genAI analysis

Another possible solution would be to apply metadata filters prior to running the documents through genAI where a metadata field is particularly relevant to the determination—such as where dates are critical to the determination.
The efficacy of genAI tools is dependent on the accuracy of the extracted text.

kp.k: Historical TAR acceptance informs, but cannot establish, AI defensibility
kp.d: The authors describe a recurring discovery-technology adoption cycle driven by expanding data, pressure on existing methods, empirical validation and eventual judicial acceptance. They recount Da Silva Moore’s 2012 approval of TAR and Rio Tinto’s 2015 confirmation of its acceptability without prior permission. However, natural-language instructions and narrative rationales distinguish generative AI from TAR, so the authors argue for separate evidence and emerging guidance rather than assuming TAR precedent establishes equivalent reliability.
qs: TAR is an acceptable discovery tool and that a producing party does not need prior approval from the opposing party or the court to implement it.
The distinctions between these tools raise new questions about reliability and efficiency that cannot be answered simply by analogy to TAR and the body of evidence supporting its use.

kp.k: Reported buyer adoption outpaces outside-counsel savings
kp.d: As contextual evidence, the article cites the Association of Corporate Counsel’s 2025 survey of 657 in-house legal professionals across 30 countries. It reports that US legal-department adoption more than doubled since 2024, with 52% already using generative AI, only 2% neither using nor planning to use it, and 91% identifying efficiency as the primary benefit. The survey, rather than the authors’ document-review experiment, supplies the claim that in-house teams were not yet receiving outside-counsel cost savings.
qs: According to a 2025 survey by the Association of Corporate Counsel of 657 in-house legal professionals from 30 countries
the study found that in-house legal departments are not yet seeing the cost-savings benefit of genAI from outside counsel.

kp.k: Broader deployment requires further empirical research
kp.d: The authors characterize their study as proof of concept and call for research across matters, document types, workflows and risk profiles. They specifically identify prompt sensitivity, generalization beyond a single closed matter and defensible quality-control measures as unresolved questions. Their prospective claim is that appropriately deployed and monitored AI may improve review speed, consistency and accuracy, with value ultimately dependent on proportionality, reliability and fairness.
qs: future studies should examine how tool performance varies with different prompts and review protocols, how well results generalize beyond a single closed matter, and what quality-control measures best support defensible use under prevailing discovery standards.
genAI may enhance the speed and consistency of large-scale review while preserving (and in some use cases improving) accuracy.
Ultimately, genAI’s value in eDiscovery will turn less on novelty and more on proof of its ability to be implemented in ways that are proportional, reliable, and fair.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Keeling, Mangum, Hanke and Ogden argue that appropriately deployed generative AI can perform first-level responsiveness review effectively, support attorney prioritization and quality control, and potentially reduce review costs; its usefulness for issue coding varies substantially by document and issue.
pts.d: The authors report 83.9% recall and 84.7% precision for responsiveness review of custodial documents using Relativity’s aiR for Review. Treating borderline predictions as responsive raised recall to 96.2% while reducing precision to 58.4%. They describe identification of responsive documents as on par with attorney reviewers, with fewer false positives, and compare performance favorably with the 70–75% recall level they describe as commonly accepted for TAR. They propose using AI to replace first-level review in suitable workflows, prioritize documents for attorneys, or check prior human coding, particularly for false positives. They do not claim uniform effectiveness: issue analysis was mixed, and they found the tool ineffective for issue coding the particular industry-specific workpapers tested. Significant cost savings are presented as a conditional prospect rather than a quantified finding. Broader adoption is framed as dependent on empirical validation, judicial guidance and standards addressing risks.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is a single-matter proof-of-concept study using actual corporate subpoena-response documents, supplemented by practice experience, earlier TAR research and case law, and an external in-house adoption survey.
pts.d: The authors, all Redgrave LLP lawyers, worked with a corporate client and an eDiscovery vendor on a closed regulatory matter. After excluding approximately 6% of documents under the tool’s extracted-text eligibility restrictions, they selected 1,600 custodial documents stratified by custodian and document type and a separate 200-document workpaper sample. Prompts based on the original review protocol were refined using small samples of fifty documents. Two attorneys who led the underlying review split the full 1,600-document set without duplicate review to establish the responsiveness gold standard. Of 559 gold-standard responsive documents, AI identified 469 as responsive; its 554 responsive predictions included 85 false positives. Another 69 responsive documents were in the borderline category, two in junk and nine in errors. Issue analysis used ten issue tags; conflict review covered 380 documents, resolving 167 fully in AI’s favor, 126 fully in the original reviewers’ favor and 87 partly in each direction. Workpaper issue testing used fifty documents and was not extended to the full 200-document sample. The authors report approximately 35 minutes of tool runtime for 1,600 documents, but provide no quantified end-to-end cost-savings estimate. Their comparison with TAR invokes published performance expectations rather than a parallel TAR run on this sample. As adoption context, they cite the 2025 Association of Corporate Counsel survey of 657 in-house professionals across 30 countries, reporting increased use and perceived efficiency benefits, but no observed outside-counsel cost savings yet.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern early-stage capabilities at the time of the study, with near-term workflow recommendations conditional on suitable extracted text, tailored prompts, human oversight and defensible validation; no fixed adoption or savings deadline is given.
pts.d: The 2026 article states that the authors understood the tested aiR products to be using GPT-4o May 2024. Findings are bounded by one closed matter and the tested tool configuration. The tool analyzed individual documents’ extracted text, excluding documents without text or outside the specified size limits, and could not use family relationships, linked-document context or metadata. Issue coding performed better when relevance could be determined from text alone and worse when it required dates in metadata, structured content, images or formatting. The authors recommend metadata filters, potential merging of cover-page and document text, checks of text-extraction quality and exclusion or separate handling of unsuitable documents. Human oversight and quality-control checks remain important. Savings depend on eligibility rates, restrictions on substituting AI for human first-level review, the extent of second-level human checking, request complexity and prompt-iteration effort. Negotiations about AI use, transparency and validation could offset efficiency gains and make review more expensive than traditional approaches. Further studies are explicitly needed to assess generalization across matters, tools, prompts, workflows and risk profiles.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are corporate litigants and regulatory respondents, their in-house and outside counsel, document-review attorneys and discovery decision-makers.
pts.d: Corporate clients may benefit from faster review, potentially lower costs and fewer nonresponsive documents inadvertently produced, but savings may be reduced by eligibility limitations, verification requirements and discovery disputes. Outside counsel and review teams may delegate suitable first-level text classification to AI while retaining prompt development, workflow design, exception handling, human checking and responsibility for discovery obligations. AI may also help attorneys prioritize review and correct false positives in earlier human coding. For matters involving workpapers, spreadsheets, checklists, linked supporting documents or metadata-dependent issues, teams may need additional human review or tailored preprocessing rather than straightforward substitution. The authors identify in-house departments as drivers of adoption, while courts and opposing counsel influence defensibility and the costs of negotiating review protocols. The article does not predict profession-wide job losses, staffing restructuring or access-to-justice effects.
